summary: God orders an initially formless earth by speaking: light and sky, land and plants, lights, sea and air creatures, then land animals and humankind. He blesses living things, gives humans an image-bearing role and food, and calls the completed six-day work very good.
whyItMatters: The opening gives the book its first picture of a good, ordered world and a shared human vocation. The seventh day that completes this sequence begins in chapter 2.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: The beginning of the narrated world, before a named human family, land, or nation.
context.literaryForm: Structured creation account with repeated divine speech, separation, naming, blessing, and day endings.

before.text: This is the opening chapter of Genesis; there is no earlier chapter to supply a prior plot. It begins with God and an unformed earth.

here.text: Follow the six day pattern from forming spaces to filling them, ending with humans made male and female and the verdict that all is very good.

after.text: The seventh day opens the next chapter, where God rests and blesses that day before the narrative turns to the garden.

outline.heading: Beginning and unformed earth
outline.note: The opening names God as creator and describes darkness, deep waters, and divine presence.

outline.heading: Light and sky
outline.note: The first two days separate light from darkness and waters above from waters below.

outline.heading: Land and plants
outline.note: Dry land emerges and produces seed-bearing vegetation.

outline.heading: Lights for times
outline.note: The heavenly lights mark days, seasons, and years.

outline.heading: Sea life and birds
outline.note: Living creatures fill water and sky and receive a blessing to multiply.

outline.heading: Land life and human vocation
outline.note: Animals appear; male and female humans receive God’s image, dominion, food, and blessing.

keyVerses.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
keyVerses.why: The first sentence establishes the scale and subject of the whole account.

keyVerses.text: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
keyVerses.why: Male and female are together named in the image-bearing statement.

keyVerses.text: God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.
keyVerses.why: The final assessment closes the sixth day and judges the whole creation very good.

questions.question: What is the “expanse”?
questions.answer: God makes and names it “sky” as a separation between waters. The chapter describes the ordered world as it is pictured in the narrative; the word is not a lesson in modern atmospheric physics.

questions.question: Why are the lights introduced only on day four?
questions.answer: Light and darkness are distinguished on the first day, while the sky lights are appointed later to mark day, night, seasons, and years. The sequence is part of the chapter’s literary ordering; it does not itself explain a physical mechanism.

questions.question: What does being made in God’s image say about women and men?
questions.answer: The statement explicitly includes male and female humans. Both receive the blessing and the commission to multiply and exercise dominion; the chapter does not reserve image-bearing for one sex.

questions.question: Does “subdue” and “have dominion” permit cruelty to living things?
questions.answer: The verbs grant humans authority over other creatures, and the next lines assign food to humans and animals. The chapter does not spell out every limit of that authority, so treating it as an unrestricted license to harm exceeds what is said.

questions.question: What work do the repeated “good” statements perform?
questions.answer: They mark successive parts of creation as fitting within God’s ordered work, culminating in “very good” when God surveys everything. The repeated evaluation belongs to the chapter’s pattern, not to a claim that later human conduct is already good.

questions.question: Does the chapter specify the length of each creation day by a clock?
questions.answer: It repeatedly uses evening and morning to structure the six days, and the heavenly lights are assigned to mark days on the fourth. Readers differ on how that sequence relates to physical history; the chapter gives no measured age of the earth.

questions.question: Why does the chapter name food for both people and animals?
questions.answer: God gives seed-bearing plants and fruit to humans and green plants to living animals. These provisions show creatures receiving a place and sustenance in the created order, without answering every later question about diet.

questions.question: Who is “man” in the image statement?
questions.answer: The verse immediately restates the created human as “male and female,” so “man” there concerns humankind rather than a male figure alone. The wording is part of the chapter’s collective account before the garden story narrows its focus.

glossary.def: The sky named by God after dividing waters in the second day’s description.
The likeness language applied to humankind, male and female, alongside their assigned role among creatures.
A repeated grouping term for plants and animals in the chapter’s ordered account.
